summary: Explains that IP fragmentation can be used to disguise TCP packets from filters in routers and hosts. It describes two methods of attack and the remedies to prevent them. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A sneaky sender chops a message into pieces so the guard doesn't notice what it is. This describes the trick and how guards can catch it.

questions: how do ip fragments bypass firewalls
what is the tiny fragment attack
what is the overlapping fragment attack
how to block tiny fragment attacks
subtitle: How chopping a packet into odd-sized IP fragments can slip a forbidden TCP packet past a router's filter, and the simple rules that stop it.

tldr.problem: Router packet filters judge each packet by its headers, but IP fragmentation lets an attacker split a TCP header across fragments so the filter never sees the fields it is looking for.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a tiny fragment attack and an overlapping fragment attack, and shows that a router can block both by dropping TCP fragments with a fragment offset of 1 (plus, optionally, checking the first fragment's transport header length).
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo with no new protocol. It gives filter writers a short, concrete rule, and it was later updated by RFC 3128.

today: RFC 1858 is an Informational memo and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 3128. Read the two together.

sections.title: Why Fragments Matter to Filters
sections.content:
System administrators rely on equipment vendors for packet filters, which keep attackers away from private systems while letting friendly traffic through. RFC 1858 argues that vendors must anticipate attacks on those filters.

The memo's abstract states the finding in one line: IP fragmentation can be used to disguise TCP packets from IP filters in routers and hosts. The document describes two methods of attack and the remedies that prevent them.
sections.eli5: Doors with guards only help if the guards cannot be fooled. This memo shows one way a guard can be fooled and how to stop it.

sections.title: How Filters Treat Fragments
sections.content:
Filters are written as if each IP packet were whole, so the user interface hides fragmentation from the administrator. One approach, described by Mogul, remembers the result of the filter for the first fragment (fragment offset FO==0) and applies it to later fragments, indexed by source address, destination address, protocol and IP ID. The memo points out two weaknesses: fragments that arrive out of order can leak through, and a router on one of several parallel paths will not see every fragment.

The simpler and common practice is to filter only the first fragment, because the interesting header information lives there. Non-first fragments pass unfiltered, since the destination cannot reassemble the packet without its first fragment.

The RFC adds that extremely small fragments are never used in normal practice, so it is safe to drop them.
sections.eli5: Usually the guard only checks the first piece of a chopped-up message, because without it the receiver cannot put the message back together anyway.

sections.title: The Tiny Fragment Attack
sections.content:
Many IP implementations let a sender force an unusually small fragment size. If the first fragment is so small that some TCP header fields land in the second fragment, filter rules that match on those fields will not match. A filter that does not enforce a minimum fragment size may pass a packet it should have blocked.

In the RFC's example the first fragment carries only eight octets of data, enough for the source and destination ports but not the TCP flags. A filter that drops connection requests (SYN=1 and ACK=0) cannot test those flags, and it ignores the second fragment because its offset is not zero.

RFC 791 requires every internet module to forward a datagram of 68 octets without further fragmentation. The memo notes that merely guaranteeing eight octets of data is not enough, since important transport fields may lie beyond the eighth octet.

Two defences are given. The direct method compares the transport header length of each zero-offset fragment with a minimum called TMIN and drops the fragment if it is shorter. Only TCP is vulnerable, because the interesting fields of the other common transport protocols lie in the first eight octets. The indirect method drops any fragment with FO equal to 1, which blocks reassembly just as effectively.
sections.eli5: The sender cuts the message into such tiny pieces that the important word lands on the second piece, which the guard never reads. The guard can fix this by refusing messages whose first piece is too small.

sections.title: The Overlapping Fragment Attack
sections.content:
RFC 791 describes a reassembly algorithm in which new fragments overwrite any overlapped parts of earlier ones. An attacker can exploit that: the zero-offset fragment holds harmless values and passes the filter, while a later fragment with a non-zero offset overlaps the TCP header and changes it. The later fragment is not checked, because its offset is not zero.

In the RFC's example the first fragment has SYN=0 and ACK=1, and the second, at a fragment offset of eight octets, carries SYN=1 and ACK=0. A receiver that follows RFC 791 rebuilds a connection request. If the receiver instead refuses to overwrite earlier data, the attacker can simply send the fragments in the opposite order.

RFC 815 improves reassembly but focuses on filling gaps and says nothing about overlaps, so fully compliant implementations are not guaranteed to be immune. The memo says the 4.3 BSD implementation avoids the attack by letting lower-offset data take precedence, but not all implementations descend from that code.

The remedy is for the router to enforce a minimum offset for non-zero-offset fragments. For TCP that minimum is sixteen octets, so a TCP fragment with FO==1 should be discarded. This also stops the tiny fragment attack, so the general rule is the one-line test below. If a router filters on fields beyond the sixteenth octet of a transport header, dropping FO==1 might not be enough.
sections.eli5: The sender sends one harmless first page and a second page that scribbles over the first page's important words after the guard has looked. The guard can stop this by never letting a second page start so early that it can reach those words.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Scope
sections.content:
The memo's own security section is a single sentence: it is concerned entirely with the security implications of filtering fragmented IP packets. The whole document is therefore the security discussion.

The attack scenarios, the RFC says, grew out of discussions on the firewalls mailing list in May 1995. The memo is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.eli5: This whole note is about keeping guards from being tricked, so there is nothing extra to add at the end.

data.title: Rule that blocks both attacks
data.code:
IF FO=1 and PROTOCOL=TCP then
        DROP PACKET
